text: AI governance is the system of decision rights, accountability, and controls over how an organization sources data for AI, builds and validates models, and takes responsibility for the decisions those models make in production. It's the same core idea as data governance, applied to a new kind of asset.

Most of what AI governance does falls into three buckets. The data going in, what trained the model, where it came from, whether the organization had the right to use it. The model itself, how it was built, documented, tested, versioned, and approved. The decisions and outputs coming out, what the model is allowed to decide on its own, what gets monitored, what happens when it's wrong.

If your organization already has a working data governance program, owners, stewards, policies, a review council, you're not starting from zero. AI governance extends that same structure to cover two things data governance alone doesn't fully address, the behavior of a trained model, which isn't written down anywhere as explicit logic, and decisions made automatically and continuously, without a human reviewing each one.

Chapter 1 stays conceptual, what AI governance is and the roles involved. Chapter 2 covers governing the data that trains models. Chapter 3 covers governing the models themselves. Chapter 4 covers security, access, and production monitoring. Chapter 5 covers responsible AI principles and named frameworks. Chapter 6 applies all of it to realistic case studies and building a program from scratch.

AI governance isn't a checklist you run once before launch, it's an ongoing set of agreements, who approved this model, who's accountable if it's wrong, how anyone would even find out if something went off track. Next up: why AI needs governance at all.
